location: That parallelism is the training pass. One pass over S tokens produces S output rows, each scored against the next token in the document; the loss averages −log P(x<sub>i</sub> | x<sub><i</sub>) over every position i. One document, one pass, S predictions. Now read the table with that loss in mind. Row 3 is supposed to predict token 4, but column 4 of row 3 holds token 3's query scored against token 4's key, and token 4's value is in row 3's mix.
finding: Toured, not explained. The explanation of the training pass mechanism contains a notation and indexing conflict between the sequence position and the predicted target. If row i represents token i's query and mixes representations up to position i, scoring row i against the next token means row i predicts token i + 1 (e.g. row 3 predicts token 4), so the loss term for row i is −log P(x_{i+1} | x_{≤i}). Stating the loss as '−log P(x_i | x_<i) over every position i' conflates row index i with target token index i. If position i in that formula were the row index, row i would be predicting token x_i from tokens preceding x_i; because causal masking includes the diagonal (column i), row i already contains token i's value in its mix, which would constitute cheating. Additionally, an input sequence of S tokens has only S − 1 subsequent tokens within that sequence; producing S next-token predictions requires an (S + 1)-token sequence or explicit start-token shifting.

In the essay's worked example, row 1 sees token 1 to predict token 2, row 2 sees tokens 1–2 to predict token 3, and row 3 sees tokens 1–3 to predict token 4.
